openers.behavior-and-decisions: Economic models long pictured people as an 'economic man', always rational and narrowly self-interested, pursuing their goals in the best possible way. This chapter tests that picture against how people really decide. Their rationality is limited, so they lean on mental shortcuts, settle for an option that is good enough, and often grab a smaller reward now over a larger one later. Controlled experiments, from games of betrayal to a shared pot of tokens, show when people cooperate and when individual interest pulls against the group. Shared standards of behavior steer choices too, and that matters for every problem in which everyone would gain from acting together.

nature-econ-034.title: Game theory: treating choices as moves in a game
nature-econ-034.text: Game theory began with a single book: von Neumann and Morgenstern's Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, published in 1944. It is the branch of applied mathematics that treats interactions between several decision-makers as strategic games. A game spells out the choices open to each player and the payoffs that result. Players are usually assumed rational in the sense of the {{ref:nature-econ-098}}. They have consistent preferences, unlimited capacity to calculate, and each tries to maximize their payoff. Games come in two families. In a cooperative game, players can make binding promises that someone outside enforces. In a non-cooperative game, any agreement has to enforce itself. A central idea is the {{ref:nature-econ-718}}, a situation where each player's choice is the best response to the others, so no one gains by changing alone. John Nash, John Harsanyi and Reinhard Selten shared the 1994 Nobel prize in economics for pioneering the field. Game theory now describes, predicts and evaluates choices far beyond markets. It is a major method for modelling competing agents in economics. It is also used in biology, political science and the study of how people decide whether to be vaccinated.

nature-econ-059.title: Homo economicus, the perfectly rational 'economic man'
nature-econ-059.text: Adam Smith wrote that we expect our dinner not from the kindness of the butcher or the baker, but from their regard to their own interest. Economic models turned that remark into a character: homo economicus, or 'economic man'. This imagined person is always rational and narrowly self-interested. As a consumer he maximizes his satisfaction, or {{ref:nature-econ-100}}. As a producer he maximizes profit. And he can think through every possible outcome to pick the best. The name came from his critics, who used it in the late nineteenth century to attack John Stuart Mill's political economy. 'Rational' here has a narrow meaning. It only means reaching one's own goals at least cost, and says nothing about whether those goals are wise in an ethical or social sense. Nor must the goals be selfish: a person's utility can include the wellbeing of family members, which fits models that stress cooperation. Two later ideas push against the picture: {{ref:nature-econ-021}}, which studies biases, and {{ref:nature-econ-022}}, which stresses limits of mind and time. Advanced theory now often uses modified agents, with limited rationality or even envy, to depict real decisions more realistically.

nature-econ-022.title: Bounded rationality: why people settle for good enough
nature-econ-022.text: Herbert A. Simon compared rationality to a pair of scissors. One blade is the limits of the human mind; the other is the structure of the environment the mind faces. Simon coined the term bounded rationality as an alternative to modelling people as perfectly rational, like {{ref:nature-econ-059}}. Three limits bind every decision: how hard the problem is, what the mind can work out, and how much time there is. So people skip the full weighing of costs and benefits. They take an option that meets their standard of adequacy, a habit explored in {{ref:nature-econ-071}}, and they lean on rules of thumb instead of strict optimization. Gerd Gigerenzer later showed that simple rules often beat theoretically optimal procedures. Kahneman and Tversky extended Simon's ideas into a map of these limits. The idea is still debated across economics, psychology, law, philosophy and cognitive science.

nature-econ-021.title: Behavioral economics brings psychology back into economics
nature-econ-021.text: In the early 1900s economists pushed psychology out of their discipline. From then on, models treated people as purely rational, self-interested decision makers, the {{ref:nature-econ-059}} of the textbooks. Behavioral economics brings the psychology back. It studies how psychological factors shape the decisions of people and institutions, and how those decisions differ from what traditional theory predicts. Its main concern is the limits on how rational economic choices really are. It looks for the places where the standard assumptions of rational, selfish people break down, cataloguing biases, tendencies and mental shortcuts. That work has a practical edge: it helps judge whether people choose well and whether they could be helped to choose better. Its models combine psychology, neuroscience and microeconomic theory. Some of its ideas are old. The notion that losses weigh more than gains appears as early as Adam Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments. Yet the field only became distinct in the 1970s and 1980s, and it spread widely after the work of Kahneman and Tversky, through the 1990s and 2000s. Nobel prizes mark its rise: Herbert Simon in 1978, Daniel Kahneman and Vernon Smith in 2002, and Richard Thaler in 2017.

nature-econ-039.title: The prisoner's dilemma: when betrayal is rational
nature-econ-039.text: In 1950 Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher, working at the RAND Corporation, designed a puzzle that still troubles economists. Two players can each cooperate for mutual benefit or betray the other for individual gain. Betrayal is the rational choice for each, yet both would get a higher payoff if both cooperated. This is the prisoner's dilemma, the basic game behind research on social dilemmas, where individual interest pulls against the group's. {{ref:nature-hist-007}} fits the pattern closely. Every country gains from a stable climate, but each hesitates to cut its own CO2 emissions. Real climate politics is worse than the textbook game, because its payoffs are uncertain, which suggests states will cooperate even less. Hardin's tragedy of the commons can be read as a many-player version, in which widespread betrayal destroys a shared resource. The game has been called the E. coli of social psychology, a standard test case for studying oligopoly and collective action.

nature-econ-027.title: Experimental economics takes theory into the laboratory
nature-econ-027.text: How do you test an economic theory? One answer is to run it as an experiment, with real people and real money. Experimental economics uses controlled experiments to study economic questions, and analyses the results with statistical and computational tools. The data are used to estimate the size of effects, to test theories and to shed light on how markets work. Subjects are usually paid in cash, so the incentives in the lab mimic those of the real world. Vernon L. Smith shared the 2002 Nobel prize for establishing laboratory experiments as a tool of economic analysis. The field sits close to {{ref:nature-econ-021}}. Leading researchers in the two tend to share techniques, though some see a schism between them.

nature-econ-073.title: Social norms: the unwritten rules a group shares
nature-econ-073.text: Many of the rules people live by were never designed by anyone. They evolved through repeated interactions between individuals. A social norm is a standard of acceptable behavior shared by a group. Some norms stay informal understandings; others are written into rules and laws, and institutions are built from many of them. Norms differ from private ideas, attitudes or values because they are shared beliefs about behavior, and they depend on context, group and history. Breaking an informal norm brings reprimands, warnings or exclusion rather than legal penalties, and the rule-breaker is labelled a deviant. A norm's life cycle runs from emergence, pushed by norm entrepreneurs, through a cascade of broad acceptance to internalization, when it is simply taken for granted. Norms also curb free riding on voluntarily provided public goods, an effect economic models often underestimate.

nature-econ-030.title: Collective action problems: when acting alone defeats everyone
nature-econ-030.text: In 1738 David Hume described a puzzle through neighbours agreeing to drain a meadow. Economists now call it a collective action problem, or social dilemma. Everyone would be better off cooperating, but people fail to, because their individual interests pull against joint action. Trouble comes when too many members chase immediate, personal gain instead of the group's long-term interest. The pattern explains things as different as the running down of resources and low voter turnout. It also describes the environmental crises at the center of this course: {{ref:nature-hist-007}}, {{ref:nature-eco-035}} and the build-up of waste. Without regulation, people and firms tend to pick the easier, cheaper option rather than the one that cuts emissions or saves resources that cannot be replaced. In a 1965 book, Mancur Olson argued that rational individuals do not automatically add up to a rational group, a claim explored in {{ref:nature-pol-044}}. For a pure {{ref:nature-econ-633}}, he argued, each contributor tends to give less as others give more. The problem is analysed with {{ref:nature-econ-034}} and through the {{ref:nature-econ-617}}, which arises whenever public goods must be paid for.

nature-econ-054.title: Heuristics: the mind's shortcuts
nature-econ-054.text: Humans, animals, organizations and even machines share a trick: simple strategies that form judgments and solve complex problems fast. These mental shortcuts are called heuristics. When information is incomplete and a need is pressing, a heuristic gives an answer that is good enough. It is not always right, and it can differ from what logic and probability would say. Herbert A. Simon introduced the idea in the 1950s, and his rule of settling for the first adequate option was one of the first models of a heuristic. In the 1970s Tversky and Kahneman tied heuristics to cognitive bias. They first proposed three: availability, representativeness, and anchoring and adjustment. Theories still differ on whether heuristics are irrational. One view sees unavoidable shortcuts for a limited brain; another sees fast methods that do as well as complex ones on less information. In a computer test of ten simple decision rules, most picked the option with the highest expected value and almost never the lowest.

nature-econ-071.title: Satisficing: stopping at good enough
nature-econ-071.text: Of 628 used-car dealers studied, 97% priced their cars with a simple rule of thumb. Typically, if a car was unsold after 24 days, they cut its price by about 3%. This is satisficing, a word Herbert A. Simon coined in 1956 by blending 'satisfy' and 'suffice'. The idea first appeared in his 1947 book Administrative Behavior. A satisficer looks through options until one is good enough, rather than hunting for the very best. Simon meant it for problems where the best answer cannot be found, because the calculation is too hard or information is lacking. The method has three steps: set an aspiration level, take the first option that meets it, and lower the level if nothing meets it in time. The behavioral theory of the firm treats profit the same way, as a level to reach, after which firms pursue other goals. Oddly, maximizers search more options than satisficers, yet tend to be less happy and more regretful about their choices.

nature-econ-070.title: The public goods game: tokens in a shared pot
nature-econ-070.text: In the public goods game, each player secretly decides how many tokens to put into a shared pot. The pot is then multiplied and split among everyone. A player's payoff is what they kept plus their share of the pot, so the game measures altruism, cooperation and free riding. It tests a theory about a {{ref:nature-econ-633}}, such as street lighting that no one can be kept from using. The theory says such goods are under-provided, because no one has a private motive to pay. If everyone were purely selfish, the stable outcome would be that nobody gives. Real players do give. In repeated rounds contributions usually slide as generous players see others hold back, but a stubborn group of givers keeps them above zero. Players will also punish non-contributors at a cost to themselves, and in most experiments this raises cooperation. Details matter. With 40 players, a multiplier of 1.03 makes almost everyone stop giving, while 1.3 keeps average contributions near 50%. Unequal starting endowments lower contributions, and presenting the game as a climate negotiation can change behavior.

nature-econ-065.title: Present bias: why now beats later
nature-econ-065.text: Present bias is the pull of a smaller reward now over a larger reward later. It means overvaluing what is immediate and giving too little weight to long-term consequences. Early models assumed people discount the future at a steady rate, a fixed form of {{ref:nature-econ-839}}. Research showed instead that people discount sharply over short delays and less over longer ones. Their preferences are time-inconsistent: what they plan for later is not what they choose when later arrives. Phelps and Pollak captured this in 1968 with the quasi-hyperbolic discounting model. The consequences are familiar. Present bias feeds procrastination, especially when acting brings immediate costs. It discourages dieting, quitting smoking and regular check-ups, whose benefits come only later. It is linked to strong urges to spend and to failed saving plans, and short-termism in general has been tied to it.

nature-econ-041.title: Anchoring: how an arbitrary number pulls a guess
nature-econ-041.text: People asked to estimate 1 x 2 x ... x 8 quickly gave a median answer of 512. People shown 8 x 7 x ... x 1 gave 2,250. The first numbers they saw set an anchor, a reference point that pulls judgment toward it even when it is irrelevant. Tversky and Kahneman described this anchoring effect in 1974 as one of the heuristics people use when estimating under uncertainty. The usual explanation is that people adjust away from the anchor too little. Scholars agree the effect is easy to demonstrate, but they still disagree about what causes it. It is also hard to escape. Even obviously wrong anchors about Gandhi's age at death shifted guesses, to averages of 50 versus 67. Anchoring appears in legal sentencing, shopping, salary negotiations and forecasting, and experts fall for it too. In a negotiation, the first price offer sets the anchor for everything that follows.

nature-econ-045.title: Choice architecture: designing how options are presented
nature-econ-045.text: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein coined the term choice architecture in a 2008 book. It means the design of the ways choices are presented, and the effect that presentation has on what people decide. Its tools include defaults, planning for error, information about results, structuring complex choices and incentives. It can also translate metrics into what people care about, for instance turning energy use into the emissions it causes. Advocates use it to steer people toward saving for retirement, healthier food or organ donation, making up for the biases that come with {{ref:nature-econ-022}}. The idea led to the UK's Behavioural Insights Team and a similar unit at the White House. It is contested. Critics say it can limit choice, undermine autonomy, or lift firm profits at consumers' expense through 'dark patterns'. Advocates reply that no presentation is neutral. Responses also differ by person: liberals and conservatives react differently to information about the environmental effects of energy use.

nature-econ-024.title: Nudges: steering choices without forbidding any
nature-econ-024.text: A calorie count on a menu forbids nothing. It simply supplies missing information for healthier choices. That is a nudge: a change in how choices are presented, designed to steer decisions without restricting anyone's freedom to choose. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein popularised the idea in their 2008 book Nudge, building on {{ref:nature-econ-045}}. Nudges work with the limits of bounded rationality rather than against them. They can simplify complex decisions by presenting information clearly, cutting the mental effort required. Making organ donation the default, with an opt-out, has helped raise actual donation rates alongside other policies. Nudges have critics, who call them manipulative, a threat to autonomy or scientifically weak. Sunstein has defended them at length. The evidence on staying power is sobering: a 2024 review reported that fewer than half of nudging experiments keep a long-term effect when re-tested.

nature-econ-052.title: Field experiments: testing ideas in the real world
nature-econ-052.text: A field experiment takes the method of the laboratory out into a real-world setting. Researchers randomly assign people to a treatment group or a control group. Any later difference then reflects the treatment rather than differences that were already there. Unlike a {{ref:nature-econ-243}}, a field experiment lets the researchers themselves control the randomization and how the treatment is delivered. The gain is realism. Field experiments have higher external validity, meaning their results carry over better to everyday life, and they can test people who do not know they are being studied. Economists use them to study discrimination, health programmes, charitable fundraising, education and microfinance. Behavioural economists turned to them partly in response to criticism of lab experiments. They have weaknesses too. Spillovers to untreated groups, people who do not comply and people who drop out can all bias results. Such studies can also be costly, hard to replicate and ethically fraught.

nature-econ-064.title: Motivation crowding: when paying people backfires
nature-econ-064.text: In Edward Deci's classic study, some people were paid for each puzzle they solved and others just for showing up. Later, in their free time, the per-puzzle group did fewer unpaid puzzles and reported less interest. This is motivation crowding: an outside reward, such as payment, can weaken the inner motivation to do a task. Against the predictions of standard economics, the drop in motivation can lower total performance. Richard Titmuss argued in 1970 that paying for some behaviors could reduce them, and Bruno Frey coined the term 'crowding out' in 1997. People paid a token amount to collect money for charity collected less than unpaid volunteers. Crowding out has turned up in teachers' performance pay, commission pay, charitable giving and student performance. It is stronger when the reward is publicly known, since people who care about looking altruistic avoid looking paid. The evidence is mixed. A 2020 review of over 100 tests found that paying for enjoyable tasks boosts performance. But removing an expected payment can leave people worse off than if they had never been paid.

nature-clim-134.title: The energy efficiency gap: savings left untaken
nature-clim-134.text: Society passes up investments that could cut energy use substantially and at low cost. The energy efficiency gap measures that shortfall: the difference between the cost-minimising level of energy efficiency and the level people and firms actually achieve. Eric Hirst and Marilyn Brown coined the term in a 1990 paper. They split its causes into two kinds. Structural barriers include fuel prices that leave out social and environmental costs, a classic externality. Behavioural barriers lie in users' own decisions, shaped by {{ref:nature-econ-022}}. High up-front costs, high discount rates, uncertain fuel prices and missing information all hold investment back. Jaffe and Stavins blame both market failures, such as imperfect information, and non-market failures such as consumer inertia. Remedies include subsidies and cheap loans, minimum standards for buildings and equipment, information and labelling programmes, and government procurement.

nature-econ-036.title: The trust game: send money and hope for a return
nature-econ-036.text: In the trust game, designed by Berg, Dickhaut and McCabe in 1995, an investor sends money to a trustee. The amount is tripled, and the trustee decides how much to send back. A purely self-interested trustee would return nothing, so a purely self-interested investor would never send anything. Yet in experiments people do place trust, expecting the favor to be returned. The game turns that trust into something a researcher can measure.

nature-econ-035.title: The ultimatum game: take it or leave it
nature-econ-035.text: One player proposes how to split a sum of money. The other can accept the split, or reject it so that both get nothing. That is the whole of the ultimatum game, first described by John Harsanyi in 1961. Its simplicity is its strength. It has become a popular tool of economic experiments because it shows how fairness, generosity and social acceptance shape real decisions, not just the drive for money.

nature-econ-025.title: Behavioral finance: the psychology of investors
nature-econ-025.text: Behavioral finance studies how psychology influences the behavior of investors and financial analysts. It assumes they are not always rational, have limited self-control and are swayed by biases. Its central question is why market participants make systematic errors. Those errors matter beyond the individual investor. They affect prices and returns, and they make whole markets inefficient.

nature-econ-026.title: Behavioral game theory: testing strategy on real players
nature-econ-026.text: Game theory usually assumes players who calculate perfectly. Behavioral game theory, invented by Colin Camerer, checks that assumption against real people. It joins game theory with experiments from economics and psychology to study strategic decisions. Its experiments test departures from standard theory, such as its neglect of altruism, fairness and the effect of how options are worded. It has been applied to interactive learning and to {{ref:nature-econ-076}}.

nature-econ-029.title: Does behavioral economics hold up?
nature-econ-029.text: Not every economist accepts that behavioral findings change much. Papers by Armen Alchian in 1950 and Gary Becker in 1962 argued that standard neoclassical analysis works even without assuming fully rational individuals. A sharper criticism concerns the evidence. Many behavioral studies fail to reproduce when repeated, part of a wider replicability crisis. Behavioral economists responded by moving from lab experiments to field studies. Matthew Rabin counters that results tend to be consistent across many situations and places. The debate remains open.

nature-econ-028.title: Neuroeconomics: looking inside the deciding brain
nature-econ-028.text: Neuroeconomics combines neuroscience with economics and psychology to explain how people make decisions. The traffic between the fields runs both ways. It asks how economic behavior can inform our understanding of the brain. It also asks how brain research can constrain economic models, such as the {{ref:nature-econ-098}}.

nature-econ-031.title: Three ways out of a social dilemma
nature-econ-031.text: If a collective action problem traps people, what frees them? Researchers group the answers into three kinds. Motivational solutions rely on people caring about others, and research finds stable individual preferences for how much people weigh others' outcomes against their own. Strategic solutions work in repeated interactions; the best known is {{ref:nature-econ-737}}, which cooperates first and then copies the partner's last move. Structural solutions change the rules of the game or remove the dilemma, as when money rewards have cut household water and electricity use. Cooperation is likelier when people can monitor each other, sanction defectors, communicate, know one another and manage resources with clear boundaries. Graduated sanctions, which start mild and let violators regain trust, support shared resource management. Yet sanction systems are costly and are themselves public goods, and rewards can crowd out voluntary cooperation.

nature-econ-023.title: Bounded willpower and bounded selfishness
nature-econ-023.text: Bounded rationality has two companions. Bounded willpower means people have limited self-control over long-term plans. It helps explain procrastination, impulsive spending and unhealthy lifestyle choices. It is closely tied to hyperbolic discounting, valuing immediate rewards more than future ones, the pattern behind present bias. Bounded selfishness means people's concern for others is real but limited. They care about fairness, returning kindness and how others fare, which helps explain charitable giving, cooperation and social norms.

nature-econ-040.title: Playing the prisoner's dilemma again and again
nature-econ-040.text: Play the prisoner's dilemma once and betrayal pays. Play it repeatedly, with memory of past moves and the freedom to change course, and the picture changes. In Robert Axelrod's 1984 computer tournaments, greedy strategies did poorly over time and more altruistic ones did better. The winner was {{ref:nature-econ-737}}: cooperate first, then copy the opponent's previous move. There is a catch. If both players know the number of rounds is fixed, the equilibrium is to defect in every round. The iterated game underlies some theories of human cooperation and trust.

nature-econ-060.title: The case against economic man
nature-econ-060.text: The perfectly rational, self-interested person of homo economicus has drawn fire from many directions. Economists such as Veblen, Keynes and Simon stressed uncertainty and limited rationality, arguing that perfect knowledge never exists. Anthropologists found that in traditional societies production and exchange follow patterns of mutual giving, called a gift economy, rather than the model's predictions. Bruno Frey criticised its stress on outside rewards and punishments over inner motivation. Feminist economists argue it undervalues unpaid care work such as caregiving and domestic labor.
